title: Pneumoconiosis
subject: Pathology
summary: Pneumoconiosis is an occupational interstitial lung disease caused by inhaled inorganic dusts. Diagnosis relies on exposure history, imaging, and restrictive spirometry. Management focuses on exposure cessation, symptom control, and monitoring for complications.

sections.p: A group of diffuse fibrotic lung diseases caused by chronic inhalation of mineral dusts that provoke a granulomatous and fibrotic reaction.
b: Restrictive pattern on spirometry (↓FVC, normal/↑FEV₁/FVC)
Chest X‑ray/CT showing small nodular opacities in characteristic zones
History of prolonged exposure to specific dusts

t.b: What is the pattern and extent of dust‑related opacities? → Grades severity; helps differentiate dust types
Does the scan show typical nodules, fibrosis, or honey‑comb? → Confirms diagnosis, distinguishes from TB or sarcoidosis
Is the defect obstructive, restrictive, or mixed? → Restrictive pattern supports pneumoconiosis; reversible obstruction suggests occupational asthma

sections.p: Severity is graded by the International Labour Organization (ILO) system and by functional impairment.
b: ILO categories 0–3 for small opacities; presence of large opacities (massive fibrosis) = Category A–C
Mild: asymptomatic, FVC ≥80% predicted
Moderate: dyspnoea on exertion, FVC 60–79% predicted
Severe: resting dyspnoea, FVC <60% predicted, or massive fibrosis

sections.p: Dust exposure is classified by mineral type; in East Africa the most common are silica from stone cutting, talc in cosmetics, and asbestos in older construction.
b: Silica – mining, stone quarrying, sandblasting
Coal dust – rare locally but seen in imported miners
Asbestos – demolition of old buildings, roofing sheets
Talcosis – use of talc‑containing powders

sections.p: Early disease is often silent; progressive dyspnoea, dry cough, and reduced exercise tolerance develop over years.
b: Gradual onset of exertional dyspnoea
Non‑productive cough
Fine crackles at lung bases
Clubbing in advanced disease

sections.p: Combine history, imaging, and lung function; ancillary tests rule out mimics.
b: CBC to detect anemia or infection
Tuberculin test/IGRA if TB is a differential

t.b: Could sarcoidosis be the cause? → Normal values support pneumoconiosis
Is there an infectious or malignant process? → Negative cytology supports dust disease

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent action.
b: Progressive massive fibrosis → respiratory failure
Silica exposure → increased TB risk
Asbestos → pleural effusion or mesothelioma
Caplan syndrome → rapid rheumatoid nodules and fibrosis

sections.p: No disease‑modifying drug; care is supportive and preventive.
b: Remove from exposure; provide respiratory protective equipment if removal impossible
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus
Bronchodilators for co‑existent airway obstruction
Pulmonary rehabilitation to improve exercise tolerance
Consider low‑dose steroids only for acute inflammatory exacerbations

sections.p: Regular monitoring detects progression and complications early.
b: Spirometry every 6–12 months
Chest X‑ray annually or when symptoms worsen
Screen for TB in silica‑exposed workers
Education on dust control and use of masks

sections.p: Several interstitial or obstructive diseases mimic pneumoconiosis.
b: Sarcoidosis – non‑caseating granulomas, often hilar lymphadenopathy
Tuberculosis – cavitary lesions, systemic symptoms
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis – usual interstitial pneumonia pattern without exposure history
Occupational asthma – reversible obstruction on spirometry

sections.p: Certain tests may appear normal despite significant disease.
b: Normal spirometry early in disease; rely on imaging and exposure history
Chest X‑ray may miss early small nodules; CT is more sensitive
Silica exposure can coexist with normal calcium; TB risk remains high

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden increase in dyspnoea or chest pain
Development of fever with cough (possible TB or infection)

faq.a: No; damage is irreversible, but stopping exposure and supportive care can halt progression.

faq.q: Why is TB more common in silica‑exposed workers?
faq.a: Silica impairs macrophage function, reducing the ability to contain Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

faq.q: Is a cough in pneumoconiosis productive?
faq.a: Usually dry; a productive cough suggests infection or another lung disease.

exam: What occupational history would raise suspicion for silicosis? — Look for stone quarrying, sandblasting, or mining; duration >10 years is high risk.

How does spirometry differentiate pneumoconiosis from occupational asthma? — Pneumoconiosis shows a restrictive pattern (↓FVC, normal/↑FEV₁/FVC); asthma shows reversible obstruction after bronchodilator.
A patient with rheumatoid arthritis and multiple upper‑zone nodules on X‑ray: what syndrome should you consider? — Caplan syndrome; it combines RA with pneumoconiosis nodules.
Why is a high‑resolution CT preferred when the chest X‑ray is normal but suspicion remains? — CT detects early small nodules and fibrosis not visible on plain film.
What is the most important immediate step for a worker diagnosed with asbestosis? — Remove from asbestos exposure and arrange vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus.
How would you screen a silica‑exposed worker for TB? — Perform symptom review, chest X‑ray, and tuberculin test or IGRA; treat latent TB if positive.
Explain why steroids are not routinely used in pneumoconiosis. — They do not reverse fibrosis and increase infection risk; reserved for acute inflammatory flares.
What red‑flag symptom indicates possible malignant transformation in asbestos exposure? — New pleural effusion or chest pain with weight loss suggests mesothelioma.
